lead: A liquid cooling loop moves heat from the engine jacket to the radiator. It can run on density difference alone (thermosyphon), on a pump (forced circulation), or under a pressure cap that lifts the boiling point. The coolant—water or a glycol mix—sets the safe upper temperature. Only a few universities teach all three arrangements at full depth. Road engines use forced circulation with a pressure cap; thermosyphon survives on small stationary engines.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for the heat path and radiator layout.

blocks.text: Hot water is lighter than cold water. In a closed loop, the column from the jacket to the radiator is hot and light; the downcomer is cold and heavy. Gravity pulls the heavy column down and pushes the light column up. Flow continues without a pump.

blocks.where: Δp is the driving pressure in Pa; ρ<sub>c</sub> is cold-water density in kg/m³; ρ<sub>h</sub> is hot-water density in kg/m³; g is 9.81 m/s²; h is the height between jacket centre and radiator centre in m.

blocks.text: The head is small—tens of pascals in a car-sized loop—so pipes are short and wide. At low engine speed the heat rate is low and the loop copes; at high speed the same engine needs a pump.

A pump, usually belt-driven from the crankshaft, pushes coolant through the jacket, radiator and heater. A thermostat blocks flow to the radiator until the coolant reaches about 80–90 °C, then opens; a bypass route keeps the pump circulating during warm-up. An expansion tank gives the coolant room to expand and keeps the pump inlet flooded. Forced circulation gives a predictable flow at all speeds, so the radiator can be smaller.

A pressure cap is a spring-loaded valve. It holds the system above atmospheric pressure and raises the boiling point. Saturation temperature rises with pressure: a cap set about 100 kPa above atmosphere lifts the boiling point of water to roughly 120 °C. Hotter coolant carries more heat for the same flow, and the radiator can be smaller. A release valve also lets air or steam out and admits air on cooling. Never open a hot cap: the sudden drop to atmospheric pressure flashes coolant to steam and scalds. A faulty cap lets the engine boil at a lower temperature; it does not add cooling.

Water has high specific heat (about 4.18 kJ/kg·K), is cheap and transfers heat well, but it freezes at 0 °C, corrodes iron and aluminium, and hard water leaves calcium and magnesium scale on hot walls. Scale acts as an insulator and can block narrow passages.

Ethylene glycol (EG) and propylene glycol (PG) lower the freezing point and raise the boiling point. A 50 percent glycol mix is common: it gives freeze protection near −37 °C (EG) and enough boiling-point margin, while keeping heat capacity and viscosity acceptable. Above about 60–70 percent glycol, freeze protection worsens and heat transfer falls. Corrosion inhibitors—silicates, phosphates, borates or organic acids—protect metals; they are consumed over time, so coolant has a service life. Use soft or distilled water with glycol concentrate, not hard tap water.

figure.caption: The loop has no pump; the pressure difference between the 80 °C and 40 °C columns drives the flow.

spec.title: Thermosyphon loop
spec.aria: Closed loop with a 0.4 m height between jacket and radiator; hot water rises from the jacket to the radiator, cools, and falls back through the downcomer.

examples.question: A thermosyphon system has 0.4 m between jacket centre and radiator centre. Water density is 995 kg/m³ at 40 °C and 977 kg/m³ at 80 °C. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find the driving pressure head. Explain why a pump is added on the same engine at higher speed.
steps: Identify h = 0.4 m, ρ<sub>c</sub> = 995 kg/m³, ρ<sub>h</sub> = 977 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s².
This small head gives gentle flow; at high speed heat rejection rises, so a pump is needed.
examples.check:
rhoc = 995
rhoh = 977
g = 9.81
h = 0.4
dp = (rhoc - rhoh) * g * h
print(dp)

traps: A pressure cap raises the boiling point; it does not increase cooling capacity.
Thermosyphon flow needs height and a density difference. A horizontal loop or zero temperature difference gives no flow.
Hard water scale insulates hot walls and blocks passages; do not treat it as harmless water.
More glycol is not always better. Above about 60–70 percent, freeze protection worsens and heat transfer falls.
Opening a hot pressure cap causes flash steam and scalds; wait for the engine to cool.

quiz.q: What drives coolant flow in a thermosyphon system?
quiz.a: The density difference between hot and cold water columns, helped by height h.

quiz.q: Why does a thermostat have a bypass route?
quiz.a: During warm-up the thermostat blocks the radiator. The bypass keeps coolant moving through the jacket so the engine heats evenly and the pump does not dead-head.

quiz.q: A loop has h = 0.5 m, cold density 998 kg/m³, hot density 980 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Find Δp.
A car boils with a new pressure cap but not with the old cap. Give the likely cause and effect.
quiz.a: The new cap may have a weak spring or a bad seal, so it holds less pressure. Boiling point is lower, and the coolant boils earlier.

quiz.q: Name the two common glycol coolants.
Why is a 50 percent glycol mix common instead of 100 percent glycol?
quiz.a: It gives useful freeze and boil protection while keeping heat capacity and viscosity acceptable. Stronger mixes transfer heat less well and can worsen freeze protection.

quiz.q: Why does hard water damage a cooling system even if it never freezes?
quiz.a: Calcium and magnesium salts form scale on hot surfaces. Scale insulates, reduces heat transfer, and can block narrow passages.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production cooling systems now use computer-controlled electric pumps and map-controlled thermostats to hold metal temperatures for efficiency. Search terms: 'map-controlled thermostat', 'coolant glycol life', 'pressurised cooling system saturation temperature'. Coolant chemistry is a large field: organic acid technology and hybrid inhibitors are common in service manuals.
